title: Gateless Barrier, Case 3: Juzhi Raises a Finger
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of embracing difficult lessons in one's spiritual practice, encouraging listeners to approach challenging experiences with an open heart and mind. This is rooted in the concept of "one finger Zen," which values commitment, steadiness, and remembering what truly matters. By cherishing painful or uncomfortable aspects of our journey, we can deepen our understanding and freedom, ultimately leading us closer to enlightenment.

sentences.text: Remembering to turn on the thing, let's take up the third of the stories in the Mumon-Kan koan collection.
If you're just joining us, I've taken on the project of giving talks on all 48 stories of the most well-known koan collections, Zen story collections.
With the third story, we encounter our first bit of upsetting violence.
There was a slap in case two last week, but in case three, things get a little more intense.
So we need to talk about that before we can hear the story, I think.
We didn't talk much about the slap in case two.
It was at the tail end of the story, which was long and involved: the story about karma, cause and effect, a little rebirth thrown in, and some animal wisdom of being born as a fox.

But at the end of the story, after the present-day master had helped the previous master be freed from his rebirth as a fox, and they had the whole thing of doing the funeral for the fox's body, remember, the master goes back to the Dharma hall and gives the evening talk.
And the style, actually, I don't know where we got this long talk style from.
I came along later.
Back then, the Dharma talks were very short.
The teacher delivers them seated on a high seat, but the assembly stands.
You don't sit down, you just stand and listen.
So when they talk about approaching the seat, that's the milieu.
You're down below, standing, for I don't know how long, 15 minutes, something like that.
Not too long.

Anyway, in his talk that evening, the teacher explains what had happened, this strange story that they had just completed about cause and effect, and being reborn as a fox as a punishment for not understanding cause and effect, or being arrogant about cause and effect.
After all that, his main disciple, a guy named Wang Bo, asked him this question: the old man, the previous guy who had been a fox, missed the turning word and was reborn as a fox 500 times.
What if he had given the right answer every time he was asked a question?
What would have happened?
And Bai Zhang invited him up to the teaching platform.

What it says is that the student, Wang Bo, actually slapped the master when he got up there, and that this delighted the teacher, who exclaimed in Zen code, "I thought the barbarian had a red beard, but here is a red-bearded barbarian."
The red-bearded barbarian is always a reference to Bodhidharma, the legendary first ancestor of Zen, of Chan in China.
I don't know that there are that many red-bearded people in India, but anyway, he was one.
So that's a really good thing to have, a red beard.
It's basically saying, yes, you got it.
So why would he say that in response to the student being that inappropriate, slapping him?
Well, Yamada Roshi's commentary says it wasn't actually reaching out and slapping him for real.
It was putting his hands and clapping close to his face, exactly slapstick.
The moment of slapstick.
But it was a moment of suddenness and a moment of directness and a moment of connection between teacher and student that the teacher appreciated.
Something about it was clear and was right.

So we might read the violence in Zen stories, and there is a bit, cutting cats in two and breaking legs and stuff like that, not as literally what happened, but more as an enactment or a play, a serious enactment.
This wasn't just messing around.
They were making a point, and with a deep feeling, or it wouldn't have been approved of by the teacher and it wouldn't have ended up in the story.
But maybe not really hitting people or cutting them or breaking their limbs.
That's a possibility.
All we really know is what the characters are.
Here are these characters: Wang Bo, slap, teacher.
Something like that.
Robert Aitken, the great American teacher who's my primary source among many, has a book on this collection called *The Gateless Barrier*.
He says we really should condition ourselves to hear it just like we hear the violence in fairy tales that we were so used to.
So we don't hear it as gross and disgusting violence, but we hear it as allegory and analogy and a part of the story.
But we stay curious about the point of the story, about the message.
Like at the end of Aesop's fable, right?
It always says, this is the point, this is the message.
It doesn't bother us that much to hear these words:
*Fee, fie, foe, fum.
I smell the blood of an Englishman.
Be he alive or be he dead, I'll have his bones to grind my bread.*
And we don't get too upset when they pop the children in the oven.
Yeah, right.
So those are a few possibilities.
But these stories present themselves, and it's up to each of us to feel our way in how we meet them.
Someone was just telling me that he's intending to take a fresh look at reading koans because they bothered him so much, but he figured he'd try it again.
So anyway, here's one that might bother you.
Case three.
*Juju raises a finger.*
Juju is the teacher in this story.
*Whenever Juju was asked a question, he simply raised one finger.
One day a visitor asked Juju's attendant, "What does the master teach here?"
So the boy raised a finger.
Hearing of this, Juju cut off the boy's finger with a knife.
And as the boy ran from the room, screaming with pain, Juju called out to him.
When he turned his head, Juju raised a finger.
The boy was suddenly enlightened.*
So, wow.
Later when Juju was about to die, he said to his assembled monks,
*I received this one finger Zen from Tangang, my teacher.
I used it all my life but never used it up.
I've used this all my life but never used it up.*
When he finished saying this, he died.
So there's much here, but we do have to work through maybe a little revulsion about this image.
I think it's worthwhile to feel the revulsion too, not just to be like, oh, isn't that funny?
It's a really disgusting thing.
But there is something powerful here about focus, isn't there?
About one thing.
Just committing.
Just practicing deeply in one way.
Dogen shares with us that to sustain one practice is to master one practice, meaning all practices.
And there's just a wonderful faith here in a steady single-minded practice, just doing it the same way every time.
Kind of like we chant the same thing every time.
But it's not the same, is it?
Right?
It's new and the same.

I think this emphasis is really helpful to us and really important, a great antidote to our endless whirling search for novelty and originality, where we all have to be more clever than anybody else and say it in a new way and so on and so forth.
Because it's hard for us even to know, I think, how much of a strain we're putting on ourselves with that, don't you think?
It's really messing us up.
But we're pretty good at it, we get used to it.
Or maybe we just are depressed that we can't be original and brilliant.
But it's a strain.
So wouldn't it be good to just really commit to not doing that anymore?
To not needing to be original or brilliant or clever, or just to do one thing.
Just to practice in one way.
Just to raise one finger.
Just to sit down.
Just to be.
But, but, there's always a but.
And yet there also is something here in how you do that, right?
It's not just doing one thing.
It's doing one thing with a certain kind of conviction and depth of feeling.
And you can't just copy somebody else.
So that's an obvious message in the story, right?
The boy copying the teacher.
That's not it.
You need to see it through more deeply than just that.
The boy of the story is just merely imitating the master but not really understanding.
The story seems to be suggesting that the boy did not really understand one finger's end until that dramatic episode.
And then he got it.
Then he didn't have a finger to hold up anymore.
So does one finger's end require a finger?
Maybe we imagine a version of the story where the master whips out his knife, pins the boy against the table, and stops just short of actually hurting him.
A kind of mock serious violence to shock the boy into seeing that his one finger's end was not yet complete.

Or maybe we do just set aside literalness altogether and see it like the giant in Jack and the Beanstalk, just a part of this wild mythological world in which brilliant masters parlay their understanding with the students in creative and crazy ways.
And it's interesting, we tend to picture holding an index finger to say one.
But actually most cultures hold up a thumb.
I remember one time in Paris, and it was late at night too, and I think we hadn't been there very long so we were a little jet lagged, confused, trying to figure out what's going on.
We had to go to this little tabac, a little convenience store, tobacco place, and I bought some little something, a map or something.
I can't remember what I bought, but I'll never forget this big gruff guy with a beard in the dim light holding up his thumb and saying [unclear: "en franck"].
It took me a minute to think about what is this teaching. [unclear: "En franck"].
I guess they'd say [unclear: "oen, oen, oen, oen"].
It's not as good because it's not really about a finger.
It's about commitment, isn't it?
It's about steadiness.
It's about remembering.
Suzuki Roshi said, "The most important thing is to remember the most important thing."
That's a good way, I think, to describe this one finger Zen.
So to ask ourselves, and to really listen to the universe, to our hearts, to really ask ourselves, what's important?
What's really important right now?
And then to dive in.
Whether we're doing it right, or understand it, or anybody's looking at us, or not looking at us, just to dive into what needs to be done, what needs to be practiced.
And at the end, as is so often the case in these stories, there's a whole second story.
Which could have been years later, they never say.
Sometimes they say "later," which could mean ten years or a hundred years.
Often they don't say any connecting words, just the next thing.
So later on, when he was close to death, the teacher in our story, remembering his teacher, Master Juzer, saying, "I received this one finger Zen from Tan Long.
I used it all my life, but never used it up."
So this understanding that what we have been offered is so big, so powerful.
What we've received from our friends, from our parents, from our teachers, from our world, it's infinite and we can never use it up.
We can be grateful, and we can remember.
I think that's part of his one finger Zen, to really remember.
And this really needs to include teachings that we don't like so much, too.
Painful lessons are also offered to us, to help us wake up.
The finger thing in the story, right, it is a painful lesson.
For some reason this made the great Indo-Tibetan teaching poem called *Eight Verses for Training the Mind* pop into my head.
The author of this was written in the tenth century.
It makes a big point that we really need to learn how to appreciate the people who give us difficult lessons.

And not just get patient with them, or psych ourselves out of being pissed off by reminding ourselves that they're suffering or something, and maybe they don't know what they're doing, but actually really love them for the difficult things that they teach us.
This is also similar to Shanti Deva's work, if you remember Shanti Deva.
This guy named [unclear: "Tian Den Langri"] or something.
Here are three of the Eight Verses.
*When I encounter beings of unpleasant character and those oppressed by intense negativity and suffering, it is as though finding a treasure of precious jewels.
May I cherish them, for they are so rarely found.*
I don't know if that's rare, but...
*When others, out of jealousy, treat me wrongly with abuse and slander, may I take upon myself the defeat and offer to them the victory.
Even if someone I have helped or in whom I have placed great hope gravely mistreats me in hurtful ways, may I view him or her as my sublime teacher.*

I'm just going to gradually ratchet that up in those three verses, ending with, even somebody I've helped, I really have a lot of love for, a lot of hope in, *mistreats me, betrays me, may I view her as my sublime teacher.* Thank you for this teaching.
So there are strong teachings in our tradition.
I think it's no good to just skip over that bit.

Although we can really for sure love and appreciate the beautiful and easy-to-accept aspects of our practice, the way that practice helps us calm down, reduces our stress, it's like a breath of fresh air sometimes to walk in here, right?
But it's also important to recognize that these teachings are designed to help us with some deep, deep patterns, some powerful misunderstandings and problems.
And so there's some strong medicine here.
And we need that.
The Dharma is also a very high commitment and high expectations kind of deal.
That's why Zen groups are never going to be mega churches.
If we want to walk the path to a real freedom, we have to actually go for it, and be willing to get hurt and be vulnerable and to work with our attitudes.
Not just accepting, but cherishing, like it says, cherishing.
May I cherish the things.
And these three verses can also refer not to people externally, but also to our own craziness.
Oh, may I cherish this stupid, messed up thought?
Thank you for teaching me about my mind.
So, another big part of the Koan tradition is that there are layers of commentary that get sort of coded around the story.
Because often, as we say, the story is pretty short and understood through commentary, like all religious traditions.
I was reading a scholarly chapter on Koans and where they came from, which I actually posted on the website.
Actually, remember to do that.
I think it's on the case one recording.
Anyways, scholars define a Koan as a unit of text that gets repeated basically consistently in the Zen literature that has commentary attached to it.
So if the story gets passed around and gets comments added to it, it becomes a Koan.
And there are different levels of status, in which collections they're in and so on.
But that's a Koan, according to scholars.
It's funny to think about, too, because it means that our commenting on Koans makes them more Koan-ful.
Or Koans them up a little bit more.
And here we're building on a thousand years of doing this, one commentary on top of another.
So we're part of a living tradition, which is nice, even if we're just messing it up a little bit more, confusing things in some way.
In this book, the actual original book is just the title, which is always four characters, the story, and then a verse.
And then a comment by Master Wu-Man.
So here's Master Wu-Man's verse on this story.
*[unclear: "Qianlong"] made a fool of all [unclear: "Juzer"], who cut the boy with a sharp knife.
Just as the mountain spirit raised his hand, and Huan Shan mountain range with its many ridges was split in two.*
So the first line is referring to the old teacher and the present teacher, that the present teacher remembers at the end of the story.
And I'm really bungling the pronunciation a little bit here, because I'm trying to learn how to do it right, which just messes me up more.
There are tones, and the intonation is very different from English.
I found this source that has the [unclear: "opinion version"] of the names with the diacriticals that indicate when it's a rising tone or a falling tone or five tones.
And you can paste that into Google Translate, and this Chinese woman's voice pops out, that I assume to be correct.
So now, instead of doing my previous approximation, or at least I'm consistent, I'm trying to remember that voice from Google.
So sorry.
You can read about it later.
But anyway, the older teacher and the newer teacher: Tian Leng, the older teacher, made a fool of old Ju Xu, the newer teacher, who cut the boy with a sharp knife.
It's just as the mountain spirit raised his hand, and Huan Shan mountain range with its many ridges was split in two.
So this, of course, turns out to be a reference to another story.
The mountain spirit is a spirit that appeared in Ju Xu's life earlier on.
Here's how Robert Aitken tells the story.
It's a really beautiful story.
He practiced in a monastery for a while as a young man, and then he's off practicing in a hut.
Who knows how old he is?
Mid-20s, something like that we'll say.
But a very vigorous practice, working hard in his practice.
Okay.
So Ju Xu is in his hut, practicing away.
*One day, towards the evening, a nun named Xichir appeared in the hut.
Her name can be translated as True World.*
And Aitken describes the characters, we'll skip that.
*True World did not knock or call out when she arrived.
She just walked in.
It was probably a one-room cottage.
Traditionally, such cottages were about ten feet square.
And there was Xichir, sitting in Zazen, right in the center.
Without even taking off her sedge hat, she walked around him three times, and then stood before him and said, "If you can say an appropriate word, I will take off my hat."*
*Circumambulation is a ritual found in traditional societies all over the world.
In Zen Buddhism, it is an act of self-presentation by a pilgrim to a teacher.*
And then we also, in our programs, present ourselves to mountains this time, too.
This way, too, sometimes.
*It is usually then followed by three prostrations and other procedures, and then dialogue.
But in this case, the nun, True World, did not observe the proper ritual, but asked him this question.
"If you can say an appropriate word, I'll take off my hat."*
Usually, you would take off your hat before you went in.
*And Xichir was unable to respond.
He was dumbstruck.
So True World walked around him three more times, stood before him again, and said again, "If you can say an appropriate word, I will take off my hat."
And again, he was unable to speak.
She repeated her performance a third time.
Silence.
She turned on her heels and walked out.
He never saw her again.*
*So when Xichir finally kind of came to himself, he went to the door,* and you can imagine, the backstory is always about a thousand hours of zazen.
So first, you've got to imagine a thousand hours of zazen by yourself.
And suddenly this person is in your face, as if out of nowhere.
So that's the backstory always.
*He kind of came to himself and went to his door and called out,* hoping she's still out there somewhere.
*He called out and said, "It will be dark soon.
Why don't you stay the night?"* Oh, she's still out there, sorry.
*She's standing outside the hut.
She turned around and said, again, "If you can say an appropriate word, I will stay the night."
He still couldn't say a word, so she left.* Now she really leaves.
*Xichir was downcast.
He had been defeated by the non-true world.
He thought to himself, "I must be going about this matter of realization the wrong way around.
I obviously need a good teacher."
So he packed up his gear and started off.
But it was soon too dark to keep walking.
So he stopped and sat on the path.
He was snoozing over his pack, cold, waiting for the dawn.
Suddenly a mountain spirit appeared before him and said, "Don't leave this spot.
A great Zen master will come here and you can consult with him."
So he stayed put.
And sure enough, in a couple of days, the Zen teacher, Tianlong, appeared.
And ended up being his teacher for many years.*
Zen always sounds so practical at first.
Meditation, you know, it's scientific.
And you don't realize it actually has all these fantastic apparitions and challenges and weird encounters.
And you never know when a nun in a sedge hat is going to appear demanding that you wake up right now and say something with clarity.
Leaning into your face, holding up her thumb.
One finger Zen.
So these stories really challenge us, I think.
Can we really show up?
Can we commit to our life, just as it is?
Not try to get some other life if we just played our cards right, but commit to the life that we actually have, and treat it as one practice.
So can we do that?
Can we really embrace and appreciate and even cherish the trouble that inevitably comes along with that?
Because that trouble is our teacher.
And sooner or later, it will lead us forward into the mountains which we'll split in two.
And mountain spirits will tell us what to do.
So don't worry.
Don't worry.
Our life will lead us to our true teacher, in other words.
So anyway, it's interesting, this commentarial tradition.
You can bring up a whole other story.
Make it into something else.
So that's case three of the [unclear: "Mu Muang calling"].
Thank you very much for your kind attention, and your steady one-finger practice.
I think happily our knives are not that sharp.
Or maybe that's worse.
